# Stakeholder Engagement Reference

Sources: REF-M05, REF-M06 ([docs/Reference.md](../../../docs/Reference.md)).

## When to Use

- Filling in the Engagement Strategy column in `stakeholder-register.md` and the user wants more
  than a generic "communicate more."
- A stakeholder's engagement has drifted (e.g. Supportive → Resistant) and the user needs
  concrete tactics, not just "escalate it."

## Engagement Tactics by Power/Interest Quadrant

| Quadrant | Default posture | Concrete tactics |
|---|---|---|
| Manage Closely (High Power, High Interest) | Deepest, most frequent engagement | Involve in decisions directly, not just informed after the fact; dedicated working sessions, not just status reports |
| Keep Satisfied (High Power, Low Interest) | Enough engagement to prevent them becoming a blocker | Periodic executive summaries; don't overwhelm with detail they didn't ask for |
| Keep Informed (Low Power, High Interest) | Regular information, limited decision involvement | Newsletters/updates; give them a channel to raise concerns even without formal authority |
| Monitor (Low Power, Low Interest) | Minimal effort, watch for quadrant drift | Light-touch, occasional updates; re-check periodically in case their power/interest changes |

## The Salience Model (alternative lens to Power/Interest)

Assess three attributes instead: **Power** (ability to impose will), **Legitimacy** (is their
claim on the project appropriate/legal), **Urgency** (how time-sensitive is their claim). A
stakeholder with all three is "Definitive" and needs the highest attention; one attribute alone
is "Latent" (low priority, but still worth tracking as it can gain the other two attributes).
Use this when Power/Interest alone doesn't capture a stakeholder well — e.g. a regulator has
high Legitimacy but may have Low/Medium apparent Power until they actually act.

## Shifting a Resistant Stakeholder Toward Supportive

1. **Diagnose the actual cause first** — resistance to "the new system" is often resistance to
   one specific gap (a missing feature, a changed workflow step), not the whole thing. Ask what
   specifically is driving the resistance before proposing a fix.
2. **Involve them in fixing the specific gap**, not just in being told it will be fixed — being
   part of validating the fix rebuilds trust faster than a unilateral announcement.
3. **Close the loop visibly** — tell them (and document in `communications-plan.md`) when their
   specific concern was addressed, not just that "feedback was incorporated" generically.
4. **Re-assess, don't assume** — after a fix ships, explicitly re-confirm engagement level with
   the stakeholder rather than assuming the drift is resolved because the gap was closed.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

- Don't apply the same engagement frequency to every stakeholder in a quadrant — quadrants set a
  default posture, not a rigid formula; a "Keep Satisfied" stakeholder who's historically been
  difficult may need more than the quadrant's default.
- Don't treat engagement level as static — re-assess every control cycle; a Supportive
  stakeholder mid-project isn't a guarantee they'll stay that way through rollout.
